questions.question_text:
Two fair four-sided dice are rolled and their product is recorded in the array.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \times & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\ 3 & 3 & 6 & 9 & 12 \\ 4 & 4 & 8 & 12 & 16 \end{array}$
Find the probability that the product is strictly greater than $6$, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Included products equal to 6 instead of strictly greater than 6.
Miscounted the number of favourable cells in the array.
Missed the product $3 \times 3 = 9$ on the diagonal.

questions.solution_text:
The array contains $16$ equally likely cells.
The cells strictly greater than $6$ are $(2,4)=8$, $(3,3)=9$, $(3,4)=12$, $(4,2)=8$, $(4,3)=12$, $(4,4)=16$.
$\text{Number of favourable cells} = 6$
$P(\text{product} > 6) = \frac{6}{16}$
$= \frac{3}{8}$

questions.question_text:
Two standard six-sided dice are rolled and their difference (larger score minus smaller score) is recorded.
Find the probability that the difference is exactly $3$, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counted ordered pairs in one direction only without considering both dice.
Missed the pair $(3,6)$ and its reverse $(6,3)$.
Confused the difference of 3 with a sum of 3.

questions.solution_text:
Total outcomes $= 6 \times 6 = 36$.
The pairs with a difference of $3$ are $(1,4), (2,5), (3,6), (4,1), (5,2), (6,3)$.
$\text{Number of favourable pairs} = 6$
$P(\text{difference} = 3) = \frac{6}{36}$
$= \frac{1}{6}$

questions.question_text:
A fair spinner has $4$ equal sections numbered $1, 2, 3, 4$.
It is spun twice independently.
Find the probability that both spins land on prime numbers, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Treated 1 as a prime number when finding the single-spin probability.
Added the branch probabilities instead of multiplying along the path.
Used $\frac{1}{4}$ for the probability of rolling a prime on a single spin.

questions.solution_text:
The prime numbers in $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ are $\{2, 3\}$.
$P(\text{prime on one spin}) = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$
$P(\text{both prime}) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$
$= \frac{1}{4}$

questions.question_text:
Liam has a $0.7$ probability of passing his history test and a $0.8$ probability of passing his geography test.
The two test results are independent.
Find the probability that he passes geography but fails history, as a decimal.

options.why: Calculated the probability of passing both tests instead of failing history and passing geography.
Multiplied the probability of passing history by the probability of failing geography.
Calculated the probability of failing both tests.

questions.question_text:
A bag contains $5$ red counters and $3$ blue counters.
Two counters are chosen at random **without replacement**.
Find the probability that both counters are the same colour, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Calculated the probability with replacement instead of without replacement.
Calculated the probability of drawing different colours instead of the same colour.
Calculated the probability of drawing two red counters only.

questions.question_text:
A fruit bowl contains $4$ apples and $5$ oranges.
Jack selects $2$ pieces of fruit at random **without replacement**.
Find the probability that he selects exactly one apple, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counted only one order ($AO$) instead of both orders ($AO$ and $OA$).
Assumed selection with replacement rather than without replacement.
Calculated the probability of selecting two apples.

questions.question_text:
A fair six-sided die is rolled $3$ times.
Find the probability of rolling at least one $6$, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Found the probability of rolling no sixes instead of at least one six.
Added $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6}$ which incorrectly treats the events as disjoint.
Calculated the probability of rolling three sixes ($6, 6, 6$).

questions.solution_text:
$P(\text{no } 6\text{ on a single roll}) = \frac{5}{6}$
$P(\text{no } 6\text{ in } 3\text{ rolls}) = \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{3} = \frac{125}{216}$
$P(\text{at least one } 6) = 1 - \frac{125}{216}$
$= \frac{91}{216}$

questions.question_text:
A safety system consists of $3$ independent alarms.
Each alarm has a $0.9$ probability of sounding when smoke is detected.
Find the probability that at least one alarm sounds when smoke is detected, as a decimal.

options.why: Calculated the probability that all three alarms sound ($0.9^3$).
Found the probability that no alarms sound instead of at least one.
Subtracted $0.1 \times 3 = 0.3$ from $1$ instead of raising $0.1$ to the third power.

questions.solution_text:
$P(\text{an alarm fails to sound}) = 1 - 0.9 = 0.1$
$P(\text{all } 3\text{ fail}) = 0.1^{3} = 0.001$
$P(\text{at least one sounds}) = 1 - 0.001$
$= 0.999$

questions.question_text:
A coin is biased so that $P(\text{Heads}) = \frac{2}{3}$.
The coin is tossed $3$ times independently.
Find the probability of getting exactly $2$ Heads, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Calculated the probability of one specific order ($HHT$) without multiplying by 3.
Calculated the probability of getting all three Heads ($HHH$).
Assumed the probability of 2 Heads out of 3 is equal to the single-toss probability.

questions.solution_text:
The paths with exactly $2$ Heads are $HHT, HTH, THH$.
$P(HHT) = \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{27}$
$P(HTH) = \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{27}$
$P(THH) = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{27}$
$P(\text{exactly }2\text{ Heads}) = \frac{4}{27} + \frac{4}{27} + \frac{4}{27}$
$= \frac{12}{27}$
$= \frac{4}{9}$

questions.question_text:
A box contains $2$ defective components and $4$ good components.
A technician tests components one by one at random **without replacement** until $2$ components have been tested.
Find the probability that at least one defective component is found, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Calculated the probability that neither component is defective.
Calculated the probability that both tested components are defective.
Calculated the probability of finding exactly one defective component instead of at least one.

questions.solution_text:
Total components $= 2 + 4 = 6$.
$P(\text{both good}) = \frac{4}{6} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{12}{30} = \frac{2}{5}$
$P(\text{at least one defective}) = 1 - P(\text{both good})$
$= 1 - \frac{2}{5}$
$= \frac{3}{5}$
